utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Your Honours, counsel and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Tecla Henry-Benjamin and Daryl Mundis, assisted by our intern Lisa Hartog and our case manager, Janet Stewart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President, good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, lead counsel and Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the other Defence, team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of the Trial Chamber I would like to greet everyone present. Now that we are resuming with our hearings, I greet the members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, Mr. Bourgon, who is hidden behind the files, but as I know he will be on his feet I'll greet him now. I also greet Mr. Kubura's Defence counsel, the two accused who are present and who are back in the courtroom after the break we had last week. We'll be hearing an expert witness today, but I would first like to address the Prosecution. Do they have all the documents that were supposed to be translated? Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, thank you very much. We have received late last week a large bundle of translations. I'm not sure yet if we have all the translations, but it doesn't seem to be a problem at this point in time, and we certainly appreciate the extra time that was afforded to allow us to get the translations. We can confer with our learned colleagues from the Defence to determine how many, if any, additional translations remain to be done but we don't anticipate a problem for the foreseeable future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can the Defence respond to the issues raised? Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President; good day, Your Honours. In response the Chamber's question, Mr. President, I would say we have received the bundle of translations, but there are others that we should still be receiving in the course of today, and we should be in a position to provide a summary tomorrow. We'll be able to inform you of the number of documents that remain to be translated. There are some outstanding documents but not many, and I don't think that this should delay the proceedings. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very well. Are there any other issues anyone would like to raise before we call the witness into the courtroom? If there aren't any issues to be raised, I will now ask the usher to call the witness into the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. While waiting for the witness, we could perhaps file the report of the expert witness, which is what we did in the case of the Prosecution's expert witness. We could perhaps tender it into evidence. This is what was done for the Prosecution's expert witness, General Rheinhardt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. Mr. Mundis. Ms. Benjamin, Defence counsel has just said that they would like to tender the exert witness's report into evidence. Are there any objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution doesn't have any objections at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, could we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is Defence Exhibit DH2044. The English version shall be admitted into evidence under number DH2044/E. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We take note of the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would like to make sure you are receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying you. If so, please say you hear me and understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear you and I understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have been called here as an expert witness for the Defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, I would be grateful if you could tell me your first and last names, your date of birth and your place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Kasim Trnka. I was born on the 16th of April, 1939, in Sarajevo, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What are you by profession? What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Currently I'm a judge at the Constitutional Court of the BH Federation, but I also lecture in constitutional law at the faculty in Bihac in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case I should call you Judge since you are a judge at the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes that is also possible, although I prefer my work as a professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, you would prefer to be called Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes because my career as a professor has been longer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Professor. Could you tell the Court what your position was in 1992 and 1993, over ten years ago, but could you tell us the position you held at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1989 I was appointed as a judge of the Constitutional Court in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Before that I was the president of the court for one year because the term of office lasted for one year. And then when the war broke out and while the former Yugoslavia was breaking up, I worked as an expert to assist with legal issues that concerned the republic gaining independence and that concerned the peace process for former Yugoslavia or, rather, for Bosnia and Herzegovina. So in 1992, from the end of April, I spent most of my time outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I was involved in negotiations, and I was part of the delegation of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina involved in discussing the peace plans for Bosnia and Herzegovina. I went to Bosnia and Herzegovina on a number of times and then again went to various meetings which were held in various European countries. Towards the end of 1993 or to be more precise in November 1993, I was appointed as the Minister of Justice in the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I remained at that post until August 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Have you already testified before a national or international court with regard to the events at that took place in your country in 1992 and 1993, or is this the first time that you will be testifying as an expert witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time that I'll be testifying before this Trial Chamber, before this Tribunal. I've never testified before a national court, but at the request of the OTP from this Tribunal, Mr. Harmon and his associates asked me with regard to Mr. Krajisnik's case to draft an expert report that concerned the establishment and the functioning of Republika Srpska. I provided that expert report. I had contract with Mr. Harmon's associates on a number of occasions with regard to this matter, but so far I have not been requested to take any part in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you are telling us that you have already drafted an expert report at the request of the Office of the Prosecution. This concerns the Krajisnik case, but apparently you have not yet testified to hearing; is that correct? Very well. Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Defence counsel who will be questioning you about your expert report, there's some information I would like to provide you with, information that concerns the procedure that we will be following here. You have said that you would prefer to be called Professor, but we note that you have been a judge at the Constitutional Court and you also said that you were the Minister of Justice in your country in November 1993. So the procedure that is followed here and will certainly not be a surprise for you, but nevertheless I will like to provide you with certain guidelines so that you can follow the proceedings without any problems. First you will have to answer the questions that will be put to you by Defence counsel, who are to your left. You have certainly met them when being proofed for this hearing. According to the procedure we follow here, which is adversarial in kind, you will have to first answer questions that will be phrased in a neutral manner, and you can then respond to them in detail. In the course of their examination-in-chief, Defence counsel may not or is not allowed to put leading questions to you. Defence counsel believes that they will need about three hours for your examination-in-chief. This means that this hearing today will be taken up by the questions put to you by Defence counsel. After that stage, the Prosecution, who are to your right, and I believe that Ms. Benjamin will be examining you, in the course of her cross-examination, the Prosecution told us 15 days ago that they would require about four hours for their cross-examination. In the course of the cross-examination, the questions put to you may be leading, and you will be able to answer them by simply saying yes or no. Then the Defence may ask you additional questions that relate directly or indirectly to the questions put to you in the course of the cross-examination. The three Judges who are before you may, pursuant to the Rules of this Tribunal, put questions to you at any point in time, but the Judges prefer to wait for the parties to put all the questions they believe should be put to you first before the Judges put their questions to you. When asking a witness questions, we have two objectives in mind. Firstly, we want to clarify certain answers that you may have provided to both of the parties, and the second objective is that if we believe that there are some gaps in your testimony, as it is our duty to try and establish the truth, we may put questions to you in the interests of justice that have not been put to you by either of the parties. This is in order to enable the Judges to subsequently gain an idea of what you meant to say in the course of your testimony. Given that you are an expert witness, the questions might be very technical, and in fact this is why you have been called here as a witness. Given the technical nature of the debate, try to answer the questions as concisely and as clearly as possible for the benefit of those who are following your testimony. If you believe that a question is too complicated or too confusing, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase the question. When the Defence said that they intended to call you as a witness, the purpose of calling you as a witness was to enlighten the Judges with regard to the general context in your country in 1992, 1993, the political context, military context, the political, social context. All these questions should enable one to understand the situation that prevailed at the time. As a result, your testimony will be very important, all the more important in that you were a judge at the Constitutional Court and you were the Minister of Justice and you are also a professor of law. As a result, we'll all be extremely interested in the answers you will be providing us with. We have your report, and we'll be referring to your written report and to the annexes. Professor, I should also point out two other things. This is something I do whenever a witness appears here. You have taken the solemn declaration. You have declared that you will speak the truth. This excludes false testimony. I don't need to insist on this. There is another provision contained within our Rules. According to this provision, if the witness believes that an answer he gives to a question may subsequently be used against him to incriminate him, the witness may refuse to answer such a question. This is a right contained in the American -- in the US Constitution but also a right contained in constitutional system. If something of this nature should occur, the Chamber may compel the witness to answer the question but the witness is guaranteed a form of immunity. According to the American system it's the Prosecution that guarantees this form of immunity, but on the basis of this procedure within this framework it is the Chamber that guarantees this immunity. I just wanted to point this out as it might be a matter of interest. It should not really concern you. So generally speaking, this is how we will be proceeding today, Professor. We will have to have a break every hour and a half. We have to have these breaks because there are interpreters who are assisting us and it is necessary for them to have a break every hour and a half, and in addition, since everything that is being said here is recorded on CDs, it's necessary to change the CDs. This is why we need these technical breaks, but it's also necessary for the witness to have a rest, because as you will soon realise, to answer questions incessantly may be tiring. And this is also necessary for witnesses to have a rest. The hearing will finish at 7.00 p.m., and we'll have two 20- to 25-minute breaks in the course of the hearing. If you encounter any problems, don't hesitate to inform us of the fact. We are here to deal any problems that may arise in the course of your testimony. You should be examined today and tomorrow. If it's necessary to continue with your testimony after that, we'll continue on Wednesday, but I think that the Victims and Witnesses Unit has taken all the measures necessary to facilitate your stay here in The Hague and to ensure that you can return to your country. This is the information I wanted to provide you with before giving the floor to the Defence. Defence will provide you with an additional piece of information. I see you have some documents before you. Don't use them as soon as a question is put to you, because in theory as the procedure followed here is purely oral, it is your testimony, your oral testimony that is important. On the other hand, if you need a document to answer a question, inform us of the fact and we will deal with the issue at that stage. It might be necessary for you to consult some notes or documents to answer some questions, but we'll deal with that when the time comes. I don't know who will be conducting the examination-in-chief. I believe it was Mr. Bourgon, who was hidden, but he isn't hidden any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I should Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. like to specify that the Defence will endeavour as soon as possible to complete the examination-in-chief before the second break. That is within a period of two hours, 30 minutes. Of course, that will depend on the answers given by the witness. Secondly, Mr. President, I should also like to point out that during the examination-in-chief I will be referring first and foremost to the report of the expert, which has now been admitted into evidence as DH2044, as well as DH2044/E for the English version. I would like to recall, Mr. President, that this report has nine attachments and that I will be using some of those attachments during the examination-in-chief. As for the documents which are currently in the possession of the expert, he has compiled three binders containing all the documents that are referred to in the footnotes in his report. Each of those documents has already been provided to the Prosecution, and I have binders with all the documents that will be used if necessary. Similarly, Mr. President, we have also provided all the parties in the courtroom, and I think the registrar can provide the Chamber with the three series of documents which are referred to and covered in the footnotes. But to facilitate the proceedings, we have provided them separately as they will probably be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Professor. We have had the opportunity of meeting yesterday and once again this morning, but for the purposes of the transcript, allow me to introduce myself. My name is Stephane Bourgon, and I am accompanied this afternoon by my colleague, Mrs. Edina Residovic, and together we represent the accused General Hadzihasanovic. Professor, I would like to ask you a few questions this afternoon which focus on your report. I understand that your report contains the specifics of your opinion, but my questions this afternoon will be in order to provide maybe a bit of the context in which you provided those answers. Are you able to follow me in your own language?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. The first thing I would like to begin with is simply to review your curriculum vitae and your experience as an expert to testify in this case. And I would like, Professor, if you could help the Trial Chamber and express what your academic background is in the field of constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours. I thank you for your questions, attorney. As far as my academic career is, I graduated from the law school in Sarajevo at the age of 24. I also acquired a masters degree at the same faculty, and in 1975, at the law school in Sarajevo, I defended my doctoral thesis on subject relating to constitutional law. After that I was elected professor at the law faculty in Mostar. During the war, of course, I was unable to teach, but immediately after the war I continued my career at the Faculty of Law in Bihac in Bosnia-Herzegovina, again teaching constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Can you help the Trial Chamber with information in regards to your teaching experience at the post-graduate level?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: I had the honour to be invited to hold several courses at faculties of law in Zagreb, Split, Banja Luka, and Sarajevo at the Faculty of Political Sciences. In addition, as I focused throughout my career on constitutional law, I have published a number of expert and scholarly papers among which I should like to underline my textbooks on constitutional law. I wrote one in 1989 and -- which covered, in addition to general theoretical questions, the constitutional order of the former state. And in the year 2000 a textbook I am still working with with my students that covers the constitutional order of Bosnia and Herzegovina today. And in this connection, I should point out that I covered the period of the dissolution of the former Yugoslavia and the independence gained by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including the functioning of the system of power in the course of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Have you published any other books or monographies on any other topics or topics related to constitutional law?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: You see, in Bosnia and Herzegovina -- or actually in the former Yugoslavia already, there was a specific category under the term "constituent people." This is a question that is not well known to comparative constitutional law, and that is why I thought it important to write a monograph on the question of constituent peoples. What prompted me to prepare this book was the procedure in the constitutional court in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1998 when I supported the proposal on behalf of the Presidency regarding the assessment of the constitution of Republika Srpska, and this prompted me to write this book. It may be of interests to note that for the needs of another university textbook, I prepared a special document on international war law, and more recently I have written several papers, and one that may be of particular interest is the one on constitutional democracy in general and particularly in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I would like to confirm your answers to the Presiding Judge a little earlier that in 1989, you were elected as a judge of the Bosnia and Herzegovina Constitutional Court, that you were the president of that court in 1990, and that after the war, in fact in March 2002, you have been elected as a judge in the Constitutional Court of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. And I am still a judge in the Constitutional Court of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Just to finish with respect to your experience and knowledge in the field of constitutional law, you mentioned to the Presiding Judge that you were for a period of time minister of justice in the government of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Have you had any other positions that you occupied around that time frame in the field of constitutional law?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: I don't know to what extent my involvement in the peace process is linked to constitutional law. I assume it is, because it was in that capacity that I participated. I was not a political figure in the negotiating process but was a sort of consultant for constitutional legal matters as of the Cutileiro plan from 1992 up to the Washington and Dayton agreements and their implementation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And finally, Professor, which position did you hold in 1994 after being minister of justice and then the next position after that?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: In August 1994, I accepted the position of ambassador of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Republic of Croatia, and I served my full term there until 1998, after which I rejoined the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina as consultant for constitutional matters until I was elected Judge of the Constitutional Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. One last question in this area. On the basis of your qualifications, your academic background, and your experience, do you believe that you are qualified to provide the expert opinion you have been requested to provide on the system of government in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the period of 1990 to 1993?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Of course it is not up to me to judge my own work, but I did everything I could to work competently, and I should be very grateful if the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution find that my report is acceptable professionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. I would now move on to the preparation of the expert report itself, and my first question would be when were you asked to provide this expert opinion, and who was the person to -- who asked you to prepare this report?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: It will be almost a year in May, because in May 2004, Mrs. Edina Residovic who is counsel in this case asked me to prepare an expert report about the questions you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you help the Trial Chamber, Professor, what was the object of the opinion you were requested to provide and what kind of instructions you were given in order to prepare this expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Mrs. Edina Residovic gave me a framework concept which she felt was needed for this case, and on a page she listed a number of theses that she felt should be professionally elaborated, and the approach mainly consisted of providing an expert opinion of the overall constitutional system in Bosnia and Herzegovina in that delicate period of time from the standpoint of the functioning of the civilian authorities and their relationship with the military authorities and finally the implications of that general framework to the situation in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, and that is what I have tried to do in my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. Can you tell us whether the report you have provided us with and which now I take this opportunity to inform you has been admitted in evidence, whether this report corresponds to the themes you were asked to cover in respect of the system in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: I think that it almost fully corresponds to my own idea, the more so as I had already elaborated that same concept in my textbooks and other papers prepared for other purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Professor, when you say almost fully corresponds, was there a part of the opinion that was added during the preparation of the report, and if so, how did this come about?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Actually, I had another consultation with Mrs. Edina Residovic when I had prepared the first draft of my report, and she thought that some matters were missing, primarily the question of regulations linked to disciplinary responsibility within the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Originally, I didn't believe that that was my task because I focused mainly on civilian authorities, and I thought that this matter was more a matter of internal organisation. So I didn't discuss it. However, I accepted the suggestion and maybe 10 per cent was added to my final report in the final version.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Can you please provide some information to the Trial Chamber with respect to the material that was used in preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: The most important materials that I used were certainly sources of law, and I am referring to constitutional law, especially the constitutional changes in 1990 when the Presidency intervened several times in that area. Then a large number of decree laws passed by the Presidency and some other regulations. I could find all this in the collection of Official Gazettes of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and this was extremely useful. I also used documents from available literature relating to this period. And finally, I myself tried to provide a clear overview, and I asked for certain annexes and tables to be made to illustrate visually the issues addressed in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In your report, Professor, you have joined nine annexes. Can you provide some information as to how these annexes were prepared and why you thought it would be appropriate to join these annexes?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: These annexes, apart from the first one which is my curriculum vitae, correspond directly to the subject matter I dealt with. I took official statistical data from the population census, particularly the one from 1991, to support the thesis that this was a multi-ethnic society and that the ethnic mix applied virtually to the whole territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I also prepared certain tables and diagrams, for instance annexes 6 and 7 have a schematic presentation of government in Bosnia and Herzegovina before the war, and I think annex 8 shows how the armed forces had civilian command, which I think is very important and that is why I provided that annex. Then there are some other annexes from literature such as maps used in the peace process, the Vance-Owen Plan, the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan for Bosnia-Herzegovina, which can also fully demonstrate the elements of the plan, and these presentations affect the subject matter discussed in the report itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. One last question with respect to the preparation of the report. Can you confirm that your report which you have given to the Defence represents your expert and objective opinion on the questions which were posed to you by lawyers for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Actually, I've already answered that question. I did my very best to provide an expert opinion based exclusively on facts. So I think all the things I have said can be supported by numerous documents and unequivocally established facts, and the references are to be found in the footnotes. And I always endeavoured to support each of my opinions with factual material.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I now move on to the first part of your report in which you discuss the manner in which the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised as an independent and sovereign state. My first question to you in respect of this section of your report is whether from a constitutional law point of view the procedure which led to the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was lawful and legal, and if you can provide the context in this respect.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: In answer to the first part of your question, I think it would be best for me to say that the international community and the European Community at the time and the member countries of the European Community, followed by the United States and a certain number of other countries, too, recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina as a sovereign and independent state. Those countries would not have decided to do that had they any doubts as to the lawfulness or legitimacy of the state independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I believe that the Trial Chamber certainly knows that during efforts to resolve the crisis in the former Yugoslavia, the conference on Yugoslavia set up the so-called Arbitration Commission chaired by Mr. Badinter, was referred to as the Badinter Commission, and the commission consisted of presidents of constitutional courts of a large number of countries of the European Community at the time. They provided answers to some highly sensitive legal questions involved in the crisis in the former Yugoslavia. And when the countries which wanted to be recognised, that is the former republics of Yugoslavia applied for recognition, all those applications were submitted to the Arbitration Commission, which provided an opinion as to whether all the requirements had been met, the requirements as stipulated by a declaration of the European Union summit, and opinion number 4 dated 15th of January, 1992, the Arbitration Commission which I will refer to later on, but it found that the pre-conditions required by Europe had been met, but they required a referendum to be called at which the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina, under international control, would state their opinion as to whether they wanted Bosnia and Herzegovina to be a sovereign and independent state. So in my opinion, these are arguments which unequivocally confirm that the course of international recognition was legitimate and lawful. As for the second part of your question, the context of these events, I should like to state in summary form as more detailed discussion is to be found in the expert report, we have to bear in mind two points as providing the context. The former Yugoslavia at the end of the 1980s and the beginning of the 1990s found itself within a process of dissolution of communist and socialist systems in Eastern Europe. A system was falling apart. And another point that certainly has to be borne in mind is that simultaneously, we evidenced a process of dissolution of a common state, and efforts were made for Bosnia and Herzegovina to acquire state independence, and on the ruins of the old system to develop a system of civic democracy modelled on countries with a long tradition of such democracies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. One more question on this topic. In your report, you discuss that the old system was founded on a single-party political monopoly, whereas this was different in the new system. Can you elaborate on the major changes from the old system to the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. new system?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: You yourself have already said that the old system was based on state ownership, which we called social ownership, of the most important means of production on a single party and a series of other elements which characterised the system such as state planning, the limited effect of the market, limited entrepreneurship, and a series of other characteristics. Of course the transition to a system of civic democracy required a change of those elements in the first place, and Bosnia-Herzegovina, while it was still within the framework of the former Yugoslavia, undertook some serious constitutional changes. This happened in the summer of 1990, when still within the old system amendments were introduced to the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina whereby, among other things, political pluralism was introduced, that is the right of citizens to freely associate, to form political parties, trade unions, associations, et cetera. Also with respect to property relations and the market, priority was given to private property, the free market, entrepreneurship. The system of protection of human rights and freedoms was developed and many other elements. I should like to point out that similar processes took place in the other parts of the former republics of the former Yugoslavia, but in Slovenia, Croatia, and Macedonia, they were able, thanks to their own political forces, to adopt an entirely new constitution which provided a complete framework for an independent and sovereign state. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, these questions, too, had started to be discussed, but the positions of the main political proponents on these matters differed to a great extent and especially so after the first multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which took place in the autumn of 1990. That is, two months after the constitutional amendments had been adopted. And the new multi-party parliament endeavoured to develop a complete text of the constitution, but their basic positions differed primarily with regard to the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And let me add, we will probably be coming back to that, according to the results of the elections, the so-called national parties, that is the parties that gave preference to national or ethnic interests of the three peoples that were dominant in the population structure of Bosnia and Herzegovina, they had completely diverse views regarding the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Serbian Democratic Party and some other parties of Serb orientation insisted that Bosnia-Herzegovina remain within Yugoslavia even though it was already clear that all attempts to reconstruct the former state, and there were various proposals along those lines, how the former state could be reconstrued, these attempts had failed to find a new model of state organisation for the former Yugoslavia. But nevertheless, these parties or, rather, the Serbian Democratic Party was in favour of preserving Yugoslavia and for Bosnia and Herzegovina remaining within Yugoslavia. However, the SDA party, the party that gave preference to the interests of the Muslims, as they were called at the time, who were during the war renamed to become Bosniaks, they preferred a solution that would preserve a common state but only on condition that both Serbia and Croatia remained in that state. The reason for this was the ethnic composition of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time when there was a large Serb population in Bosnia-Herzegovina and also a large body of Croats, whereas the majority was in Croatia, the majority of Serbs in Serbia. So the interests of Bosnia-Herzegovina was to establish a favourable balance between Bosnia-Herzegovina and these neighbouring states. So the crisis broke out when it became clear that the unified state could no longer function and when Croatia and Slovenia had covered much of the path to independence. So the end of 1999 was spent in these difficult discussions about the possible constitutional solutions for Bosnia-Herzegovina. The constitutional commission of which I was a member in 1991 did prepare a model of the constitution. Unfortunately, all the key points of that draft provided for several alternatives which showed that no unified position could be developed regarding the future set-up of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now for a shorter question in terms of: Did the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina hold a referendum, what was the result of the referendum, and did Bosnia gain its independence and when?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: This issue is dealt with at length in the report, of course, but very briefly I would like to emphasise the fact that when the European Community established the criteria according to which new states could be recognised, it was necessary for each interested country to make an application fairly rapidly. I don't have time to go into all the details that preceded that event, but up until the 25th of December, which was the deadline by which this should be submitted, there was a meeting of presidents in Bosnia-Herzegovina which was -- at which this application was submitted with all the necessary documents for such an application. Unfortunately, the representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party, the SDS, who in the Presidency and in the government who participated in the Presidency and the government didn't want to support the application. Although they had already previously organised structures of power in Serbian municipalities, in the so-called Serbian municipalities and Serbian autonomous regions. And finally on the 9th of January, 1992, they declared the existence the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which in August 1992 was renamed and called Republika Srpska. The SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party, had already started working on the destruction of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because they wouldn't accept the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The arbitration commission established that Bosnia-Herzegovina met the conditions as far as protecting human rights are concerned and as far as other issues are concerned, but they came to the conclusion that the Serbian representatives had not participated in drafting the application. And then on the 15th of January, 1992, they stated that at that point in time, in Bosnia and Herzegovina had not met the conditions for international recognition, and this is the key sentence. This opinion could be changed if the authorities, if the government in Bosnia-Herzegovina holds the referendum under international control, a referendum to which all the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina will be called to and he the question as to whether they are in favour of a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina. Sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina. On the 25th of January, 1992, the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina issued a declaration on holding a referendum which was held on the 29th of February and on the 3rd of March, 1992, under international control, of course. It's interesting to note that the constitutional definition of Bosnia-Herzegovina was contained in the question put at the referendum, and the question was as follows: Are you in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a sovereign state of citizens, equal peoples - and then they listed the peoples, the Muslims, the Serbs, and the Croats, and other ethnic groups - are you in favour of this state being independent? Naturally the SDS, the Serbian Democratic Party tried to convince citizens under its influence not to participate in the referendum, but the participation of the citizens in the referendum confirmed the fact that about 63 per cent of all those who voted in the referendum were in favour of the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a state. On the basis of the results of the referendum, the European Community and its Member States in April 1992 recognised Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the 6th of April, that was done as far as Slovenia and Croatia were concerned. Macedonia had problems with Greece because of the name. Macedonia on the 7th of April was recognised by the USA, and that's how Bosnia and Herzegovina was recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. Moving on to the period or something you mentioned a little earlier concerning the SDS who adopted the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Can you explain what was the process used by the SDS, and what happened to this project before the constitutional court of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Since the main constitutional ideas differed among the political parties at elections in 1990, the SDS, in autumn -- as of autumn 1991, had already started creating para-states, Serbian municipalities, Serbian autonomous regions and, later on in November, the Assembly of the Serbian people of Bosnia-Herzegovina was also formed. In order to show that this Assembly was legitimate, deputies elected in 1990 at the parliamentary elections were asked to withdraw from the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and to form an Assembly of the Serbian people. That was an Assembly that consisted of one nation. In addition to the SDS, there were two deputies from the Serbian Radical Party. So in fact, they established de facto authority in contravention of the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is what the Constitutional Court declared in its decision of autumn -- in the autumn at the proposal of the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's interesting to note that there was a similar situation with the Croatian Democratic Union, the HDZ, because the HDZ ostensibly supported the independence and sovereignty of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but at the same time they formed institutions which were called cultural -- which were called a cultural and economic community. But in fact it acted as a de facto authority in certain areas where the Croatian population was in the majority but not always in the majority. There were other criteria that were in force too. But in the autumn 1991, at the same time that a legal system of power was established, there were para-state formations that were formed under the SDS and under the HDZ.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Now, can you help the Court - help the Trial Chamber, sorry - in explaining what was the constitutional impact of the Constitutional Court about the projects and decisions adopted by the SDS and the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: To answer the question, one should bear in mind certain things. One should make a distinction between the legal consequences and the factual consequences from the point of view of law, national and international law, these entities were illegal entities because they had not been created in accordance with the constitution which was what was established by the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In any case, from a factual point of view, it in fact had no direct effect because those who had created these para-state entities didn't pay much attention to the decisions of the Constitutional Court. They continued to pursue their projects. And as far as the SDS activities are concerned, this culminated in the declaration of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina subsequently renamed Republika Srpska. And the HDZ, after a certain period of time, renamed this community and called it the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And a decision of the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina also exists with regard to this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Professor, from a legal point of view, what is the validity of any laws or decree laws or any other legal text adopted by the authorities of either the SDS and the Serbs and the HDZ and the Croats?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Since there was a military force behind their decision, standing behind their decisions and since the organisation of those entities included the organisation of armed forces, this means that the armed forces ensured the de facto implementation of their decisions. But on the other hand, in the light of what I have already said, it's quite clear that this couldn't be accepted by the local legal system and international -- the international legal system couldn't accept it either. And as far as the Croatian republic of Herceg-Bosna is concerned and Republika Srpska later on, if we carefully analyse the peace agreement with Bosnia-Herzegovina, better known as the Dayton agreement, we will see that that agreement, too, does not recognise the Republika Srpska as such. The Dayton agreement requires that the de facto constitution of Republika Srpska at the time should be brought into line within three months with the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina that was confirmed in Dayton. The reasons for this why quite clear, and Republika Srpska really did have to change to a significant extent its initial constitution. I'd just like to point out that for example, in the first draft of the constitution, Republika Srpska ti said that it was an independent state of Serbian people and of members of other peoples. Naturally, when you compare this with the Dayton constitution, but that doesn't concern this dispute, then Republika Srpska is an entity. It's not a state, it's an entity according to the constitution. And it's not just an entity belonging to the Serbian people. Bosnia-Herzegovina is the state of Bosniaks, Croats, and Serbs, and members of other ethnic groups including the citizens of Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is just a digression to explain what the initial situation was in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I would now like to move on to the existing structure of the authorities on the level of the state, and that is the socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the period of 1990 to 1992. My first question in this regard is how many levels of government were there in the SRBiH during the period of 1990 to 1992?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: There were only two levels. There was the state level with the relevant institutions at that level. And I should like to emphasise the fact that the content and organisation of the structure of power had in fact been significantly changed as opposed to the idea of the single power system, a single party system which was the former system. As of 1990, the idea of a division of power as far as the legislative [Realtime transcript read in error "logistics"] of executive and judicial authority was concerned was accepted. So these institutions functioned on the principle of the independence of power, was consistently implemented more or less. To a significant extent, this division of power was respected. There was another level which was the municipal level. Municipalities that hadn't significantly changed in the 1990s apart from the fact that the multi-party system was adopted, in municipalities there was a significant degree of independence. In addition to acting as an organ of executive power of the state organs [Realtime transcript read in error "arrogance"], it had a high degree of independence of when it came to local issues. It's perhaps not necessary to point out the fact that some towns such as Sarajevo didn't have that much significance on the organisation of power. Only Sarajevo had the status of a town with a number of municipalities. It consisted of a number of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Before I go on, Professor, I would just like to make two corrections to the transcript first on page 29, line 18, we see the word logistics, and my understanding is that the correct word should be the legislative, the executive and the judicial. And the second correction I would like to make is at page 30 line 1 where the word arrogance I believe should be the word state organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I wanted to draw your attention to these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's 25 to four. As I said a while ago, we will have our technical break and we will resume at about 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume and I give the floor to Mr. Bourgon is to continue with his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Welcome back, Professor. When we left before the break, you mentioned in response to one of my questions that in 1992, there were two levels of government in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, namely the municipal level and the state level. What I would like to do at this point is to refer you to annex 3 of your report and ask you to comment on this annex 3 in terms of the structure of the authorities on the level of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1990. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, if necessary, the witness could put the annex on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Professor, I would simply like you to, using the appointment and attachment 3 in your language on the ELMO, to point at each box and provide some background information to the structure of authorities.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: I've placed the English version on the ELMO, in fact. As I was saying, the structure of the authorities was based on the division of power. The legislative power was in the hands of the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The parliament, which was elected by the citizens directly. These two levels of power were represented in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. We have the council of citizens, the citizens directly elected deputies, and there's the council of municipalities, the municipalities represented on an equal basis and the citizens also directly elect one representative from each municipality. Both Chambers of the parliament take decisions on an equal footing. And then we have the executive authorities formed by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, including ministries and other agencies. In the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in accordance with the principle of the division of powers, it has legitimacy because all the citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina elected seven Presidency members at the elections, and in that institution there is the principle of equality of the three constituent peoples, at the time the Croats, the Muslims, and the Serbs. Although the percentage they represented in the population is quite diverse, as you are well aware. And then there is one member of the Presidency who didn't declare himself to be a member of any of the three constituent peoples but described himself as a member of other peoples. As far as the Presidency is concerned, there is the chief of the state. It represents the head of state. It's of great importance in peacetime but especially in wartime. It has great importance and has an expanded composition. And finally there are the judicial authorities which forms a sort of pyramid. There's a pyramid. You have first level and second level institutions, and you have the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And as usual, they have jurisdiction. They're competent to deal with criminal and civil proceedings. It depends on their actual and territorial jurisdiction. And then there is another special institution. It's the Constitutional Court. Some call it the fourth body of power, but naturally its primary role is to ensure that the constitution is respected. In our case, it also had to ensure that the law was abided by, and it also had certain other competencies. Judges from the Constitutional Court were appointed by the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the proposal of the Presidency. So there was the Constitutional Court and its structure. As I was a member of the court at the time, it was balanced in terms of its national composition, and at least formally speaking it was professional. It was a professional body, because out of nine judges there were eight Ph.D.s. So that would be the main scheme of the structure of the authorities in peacetime when one expects that all these institutions of power, all these bodies of power function normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, you mentioned that the second level of authority in that period was the municipal level. How would the municipal level of government compare with what you see in annex 3 of your report in terms of what organisations would you find at the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: A minute ago I said that municipalities had two functions. Firstly to carry out decisions of the institution -- institutions of power at the level of the state; and secondly, they were involved in local self-management. They played these roles within an organisational system that consisted of municipal assemblies. These were, let's say, legislative bodies or representative bodies because the municipality doesn't pass laws. It adopts decisions. They had the Statutes as the most important document for the organisation of the municipality. And deputies in municipal assemblies were directly elected by citizens. Municipalities had their Presidency, and these presidencies had an important role to play when an imminent threat of war had been declared. And the Presidency in peacetime doesn't have a significant role, in fact. It was the Executive Board that had executive power, and it's analogous to the municipal body of power. The Executive Committee consisted of heads of various departments. I won't say ministries. That's not what they were called. They were called secretariats. For example, there was one for economy, for finance, for housing issues, for town planning, et cetera, et cetera. And the Executive Committee, apart from carrying out the decisions of the Municipal Assembly, was also responsible for coordinating various state administration organs, because the heads of those organs were at the same time members of the municipal executive committees. Independently, the judicial authorities were independent of these structures, and the low court, the so-called basic court, that's how it was called, as a rule covered one or several neighbouring municipalities, because not each municipality had such a low -- a lower court. But municipalities in the vicinity of a town would usually be covered by one municipal court. I will also mention the -- the organisation in courts, although that's something I have referred to in my report. There were higher courts which could be either first level or second level, appeal courts, when they dealt with appeals against decisions of first-level courts. Then there was the Supreme Court at the top of the pyramid that represents the judicial system in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can you explain when this annex 3 reflects the structure of the authorities immediately prior to Bosnia and Herzegovina gaining its independence, that is in April of 1992? Was this the way the system worked?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: This was the structure of the authorities as stipulated by the constitutional amendments of 1990. It doesn't differ significantly organisationally, but substantially it did because on the basis of the multi-party system after the elections, the structure of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the municipal assemblies reflected the political feelings and inclinations at each level, the level of each municipality. One should not forget in the interest of explaining the genesis of this whole matter that the constitutional development of the former Yugoslavia was marked in particular by 1974 when the new constitution was passed for that country and its republics, and this constitution strengthened the position of the republics as states and at the level of Yugoslavia a number of confederative elements were introduced. So this was a forerunner to the subsequent break-up of the SFRY because the republics were fully equipped institutionally and personnel-wise with the exception of the military structure which continued to be highly centralised, and of course the single-party structure which continued to be centralised. As to other forms of the system, they had a high degree of independence and according to the constitution of Yugoslavia and their own constitutions they had characteristics of statehood, and there was a basic constitutional principle that all rights should be realised in the republics and only those which the republics voluntarily deferred to the federal state should be realised at the level of the federation. Whereas in the institutions of the common state such as the Presidency and the Chamber of peoples in the Assembly, there the republics were represented on a parity basis. Republics as well as the autonomous provinces. With respect to vital issues, a consensus had to be achieved among all six republics and two autonomous provinces. So all this preceded the gaining of independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina and some other former republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: The next issue that you cover in great detail in your expert opinion is the changes that took place in the structure of the authorities upon a declaration of an imminent threat of war. My first question in this respect is that on 8 April of 1992, when this declaration of an imminent threat of war was made, we see that the SRBiH or the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina became the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that the "S" disappeared. Can you explain why this took place?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: First of all, the immediate threat of war was proclaimed because on the day of the international recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the 6th of April, extensive, organised, and very forceful attacks were launched by the Yugoslav People's Army supported by military units of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the army of the Bosnian Serbs against towns and other targets of interest to them. That is why it was essential to declare a state of imminent threat of war, and that is what the Presidency did. In fact, only two days after the beginning of those military operations. The constitutional project that had already been envisaged, and this is not unknown in other constitutional systems, that in the case of emergencies, the system is adjusted to respond to those extraordinary circumstances. The first thing that happens is that the parliament is unable to function, and its prerogatives are taken over by the executive branch of government, in this case the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which for that purpose is enlarged by the addition of the president of the Assembly, the Prime Minister of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and the commander of the republican staff, as it was known at the beginning. Later on we will see that it was significantly transformed. So these added members enjoy equal status as the original members of the Presidency, if I can call them that. Perhaps more significant than the actual membership are the competencies of such an enlarged Presidency, because they acquire very wide prerogatives and the Presidency is authorised not only to amend existing laws and regulate certain areas, but it also is entitled to change certain provisions of the constitution but not all of them. This enlarged Presidency also had the authority to elect and appoint individuals which would normally be done by parliament. So this was extremely important. And of particular importance in such situations of an imminent threat of war, the Presidency acquires a more important position with respect to the civilian control over the armed forces. Later on, this institution of civilian authority was further elaborated through constitutional amendments and the passing of other regulations relevant to this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, Professor, before we move on to annex 6 of your report, which I believe illustrates what you have just said, I have one question concerning an issue raised on your report and that is the level of the district, because earlier you mentioned there were two levels, but I believe in your report you mention a third level which is that of the district. Where does that fit in in the organisation of the authorities?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: A moment ago, I said that there were two levels, but we were talking about peacetime conditions, that is municipal and state level. However, even according to the regulations of the former Yugoslavia, that is while Bosnia and Herzegovina was still a part of the former Yugoslavia, a situation was provided for when in the event of an imminent threat of war or a state of war, it is possible to form an intermediary level of authority, and we shall see later that that is what actually happened in August 1992 when a decree law was passed on the formation of districts. And the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina was divided up first into seven districts, later on into ten, which had as their aim in line with the general principle that I mentioned at the beginning that the system had to adjust to the newly created situation and the whole structure is mobilised in defence of the country. Such a move, such a development is welcome, that is the development of a district, because it will allow more effective defence. The first reason being that the authorities of the State of Bosnia-Herzegovina can more easily communicate with seven or ten districts, because in wartime conditions, communications are difficult; and secondly, such regional structures are better suited to the specific situation that may develop in certain regions. And the focus and main requirement in favour of forming such districts was to mobilise primarily civilian entities to do everything in their power to strengthen the country's defences. True enough, at the beginning the military structure will also be adjusted to this structure, but we will see later on that the military structure was gradually separated from the civilian structure and a separate line of command -- chain of command was established going from the Presidency to the smallest unit of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... go to annex 6 of your report, which describes the scheme of civilian control over the armed forces of the republic. I would ask that you place the version of this annex in your language on the ELMO and that you explain to us how this system worked.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: In this annex, we see the composition of the enlarged Presidency. So that in addition to the seven directly elected members, there were three other members attached on an equal footing. But what is even more important is the influence of the Presidency over the other structures of authority. And we will see that this top segment, which has to do with the military chain of command, and a second segment, that is the Ministry of the Interior, and through them relations with other civilian authorities. When talking about the functioning of the civilian command over the armed forces, which is certainly one of the most sensitive and most important questions of any democratic state that legitimately controlled bodies should have control over the use of military force, and that structure goes through the defence ministry, and in the defence ministry we have to distinguish between the position of the minister and the position of the Territorial Defence Staff of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as it was called at the beginning, which was later renamed to the Supreme Command Staff. From the Supreme Command Staff, the chain of command at first went towards the staffs, defence staffs of districts and municipalities, which were also within the defence secretariat. And later in the course of 1993, the chain of command went directly through the military structure, through the corps to lower-level military units. When talking about the armed forces, apart from the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was the core of the armed forces and the main component of the armed forces, a component of the armed forces are also the police and some other important structures, in point of fact, all persons who are officially under arms. But the situation with the Ministry of the Interior or the police differs significantly from the military structure consisting of the army and its chain of command. The police and the Ministry of the Interior is a civilian body, and in principle it is responsible for the maintenance of law and order, for the regulation of civic relations, for the maintenance of the constitutional order in the civilian sense, whereas the time task of the military structure is to defend the country from external attack but also, should there be a rebellion or any other kind of military pressure against the country it is responsible for that, too. And it is very important to distinguish between these two chains of command, civilian command over the armed forces, the army, and civilian control over other segments of the armed forces, and the police in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I would now like to move to annex 7 of your report, which I believe describes the structure of authorities at the district level. And if you can place the annex 7 in your language on the ELMO and explain to us how the authorities function at the district level.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: The general principles that I have described for the functioning of the authorities were implemented at district level as well, so that at Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the level of districts, there was a body which is in a sense a legislative body, though even districts don't pass laws. They pass decisions. Since districts only exist in wartime, there's no possibility for the citizens to directly elect deputies to the district Assembly, and that is why this Assembly for reasons of legitimacy is derived from municipal assemblies, the composition of which were deputies legitimately elected at elections. Therefore, every Municipal Assembly, which means the municipal parliament, delegates a certain number of deputies to become members of the district Assembly or parliament. In view of the fact that the district Assembly is a rather bulky body which is not always able to meet in wartime, the Presidency of the district is formed composed as indicated here, and when the Assembly is unable to meet the Presidency carries out the duties of the district Assembly. Then there is also an Executive Board which acts as the government at the district level, and it has heads of state administration bodies, but in the case of districts and in wartime, these bodies are quite narrow, so there has to be at least four secretariats at the district level, and some districts, probably the more developed ones, could form additional secretariats but upon permission from the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In districts, we also have special organs, and I think they are particularly interesting from the standpoint of what we are discussing here. We have a district defence staff which is vertically linked to the Supreme Command Staff, and it continued to function up until June 1993, after which this position was taken over by corps because the military chain of command was by then completed. Then we had the Civil Defence staff, which was not under the jurisdiction of the Supreme Command Staff but, rather, under the jurisdiction of the republican Civil Defence Staff. And this again is a civilian body focusing more towards the democratic district bodies and vertically linked to the Civil Defence staff at the level of the republic. I wish to draw attention in particular to what I was saying a moment ago, and that is the police structure. The police structure was organised within the Ministry of Internal Affairs of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was centralised for the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And at the regional level, there were security services centres. You will note that these centres are not called district centres but simply security services centres, though as a rule their area of responsibility did coincide with the territory of the district, and the actual operative body which is part of this police system is the public security station or what we know as a police station which exists in every municipality, and in larger towns there can be several police stations. What is important is that from the police station through the security services centre right up to the Ministry of the Interior there's a centralised, vertical chain of command and communication. True, police organs and security services centres also have horizontal contacts, but they do not receive orders from regional or local authorities but are only duty-bound to provide those authorities with so-called security information about the security situation in a particular area. And if these district or municipal bodies have any initiatives in that respect, it is their duty to address those initiatives to the Ministry of the Interior which will, if necessary, pass on that initiative down their chain of command. And finally, we have the communications and information centre, which is a centre for technical matters. And I didn't really delve into their own competencies, but the name itself speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I would now like to come back to annex 3 of your report and to look at the second organisational chart included in the report, the one which displays the structure of civilian and military organs in Travnik in 1993. I would ask that you take the version of this annex in your language and that you place it on the ELMO. The second one, yes. Now, in respect of this particular annex, without going through every part of the annex, I would first ask that you explain the organs of the Travnik municipality going downwards.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Before that, I think it would be a good idea to say that this is an even more complicated chart, which includes the functioning of the military structure going from the Presidency down to Travnik municipality, then the civilian structure. And on the right-hand side of this chart we have the de facto authorities of the HVO, which was developing its own parallel structure of both civilian and military authorities. However, that structure did not come under the jurisdiction or civilian control of the Presidency. It had its own chain of command going from the Presidency of the Croatian Community, later the Republic of Herceg-Bosna through staffs right down to the HVO military units. And I believe Your Honours have had occasion to learn about this. The Croatian Defence Council or the HVO was a specific entity, in my view unknown in democratic systems when both the civilian and the military component were united organisationally and personnel-wise. So the HVO at the level of the whole of Herceg-Bosna and later at the level of each municipality where they had power combined both the civilian and the military powers. To highlight the specific situation in Travnik, we have to take note of a new category for this whole story, and that is that since a large part of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina was under the de facto control of Republika Srpska and de facto control of the Croatian Defence Council and that military operations were ongoing throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the legal authorities treated these territories as occupied territories. And in the documents of the official authorities, when the state of war was proclaimed, it was noted that 70 per cent of the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina was under the de facto control of these para-statal entities. Of course, every legal government, and this is part of international law, does not recognise occupation, and that is why it forms institutions for those areas as well. But as those institutions of authority cannot function at all in those territories, we have what are known as dislocated institutions of authority. And Travnik may be a good example of this, because since the district of Banja Luka was under the de facto control of Republika Srpska and since this area consisting of some 12 municipalities leaning on Banja Luka and that were in the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, there was a massive influx of refugees. We can't call them refugees because they're in their own countries. Displaced, persons, rather, who arrived in the territory under the control of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And that is where these dislocated bodies were formed consisting of all the authorities that I described when talking about districts and municipalities, and when legislative, executive, and judicial bodies had to be formed, and soldiers know this better than me, including military structures that had the attributes of being from occupied territories. So this chart shows how sensitive the situation was with respect to the functioning of the system coupled with the problems that we had in communications with the central authorities in Sarajevo who were under siege throughout the war so that communication with the authorities in Sarajevo was extremely difficult, in some situations quite impossible. If you may have any specific question about this, I would be glad to and he. I think to explain each of these details would take a lot of time. I think it is the principle that matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Professor, if I look at this chart, can you explain in what way this chart illustrates the fact that the military is under civilian control and that the military is also separate and distinct from the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Well, this chart in fact displays the vertical relation, so to speak, in colours, and there's the civilian vertical that's also represented. The military structure goes through municipal and district staffs towards the Supreme Command Staff or, rather, through the Supreme Command Staff up to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is without doubt a civilian body that was legitimately elected. Later there would be changes that I have already mentioned. As the armed forces were built up, it gradually became less necessary to form district and regional staffs -- and municipal staffs and they would disappear by the summer of 1993. And the chain of command was -- only went through the corps and the brigades. I don't know what the names of all these military formations are, but it was an exclusively military chain of command. So even units formed of citizens from the territory of, let's say, the Banja Luka district, even they were under the direct control of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. On the other hand, the civilian bodies, with regard to the Ministry of the Interior, also had vertical relations. And as far as the other bodies of power are concerned, the situation was a little more particular. There was a relation of subordination when it came to carrying out state rules and regulations. And there was a degree of autonomy when it came to the responsibility of a district or the constitutional responsibility of a municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: To be a little bit more specific, Professor, I would just like to use one example which would be that of the CSB Banja Luka, which appears to have a line upwards, vertical relationship to the Ministry of the Interior, and at the same time a relationship to the Banja Luka district. Can you explain a little more the difference between those two lines?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Well, in fact it all has to do with the territorial or personal application of law. Here we're dealing with the personal application of law. The MUP, the Ministry of the Interior or, rather, the CSB in Banja Luka, the security services centre, is vertically related to the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo, to the M-U-P, the MUP. But it has personal responsibility for the displaced population from Banja Luka, or rather from the Banja Luka region.
