Whereas the Travnik CSB, which is also linked to the MUP in Sarajevo, has territorial responsibility for all issues that the MUP would usually be responsible for. So this is a specific situation that we encounter in wartime, and it is not customary in law. Territorial elements and -- elements of the territorial application of law and of the personal application of law are combined.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. A question related to the civilian police. This chart illustrates or does not provide any line of command and control from the military to the civilian police. Was that always like that or was it possible for the military, the army, to exercise command and control over the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: If you look at the system, naturally I can't talk about factual cases that I'm not familiar with, but if you look at the system in force and given what I could see in the documents, it wasn't possible for the army to influence the civilian police. On the contrary. A number of documents demonstrate that it was clearly understood that there was a difference between the responsibility of the civilian and military police, between military units and civilian police units. They were held accountable in different ways. The line or the chain of command was different. When they had a joint task to carry out, then there were joint orders from the military and from the civilian authorities on forming, let's say, joint patrols consisting of members of the civilian and of the military police. It would be stated that the military police would only be responsible for members of the military, whereas the civilian police would be exclusively responsible for civilians. So in the documents that I had, I didn't come across any information according to which the army influenced the police force. Naturally, if there were any incidents, I know nothing about that, but that does not affect the principle that I have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Professor, wrote it have been possible to subordinate the civilian police to the army?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Only in exceptional circumstances would that occur. And since we're dealing with irregular incidents, then there must be a decision of the Presidency, the Supreme Command of the armed forces, according to which in some military operation certain police forces will be engaged. But as far as I understood, the Presidency had to clearly define the event, the contingent, the force, and the participation and how the participation of the military police in an operation would take place. And in such a case, the police -- armed police forces would be subordinated to a given military unit, but naturally this was always treated as an exceptional situation given the distinction of responsibilities of the civilian and military bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I would like to cover on this chart before moving on, and that is the Municipal Staff of civilian protection. I would like to know whether this organisation is a civilian or a military organisation, what its duties are, and to which organisation is it accountable to.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: As the term itself says, the term "civilian protection," this body is a civilian one, a civilian body which functioned and existed both in peacetime and in wartime. It still exists today. There is a civilian protection system, and it's responsible for providing the civilians with all forms of assistance, to provide them with shelter if war breaks out, to protect cultural and historical monuments, to clean up the terrain after military operations have been conducted, to supply the citizens in such exceptional circumstances. It had a series of such civilian tasks to be carried out. Then and today, too, members of the civilian protection had different characteristics. They never wore military uniforms. They always wore blue overalls and carried out the work they had to do. In an organisational sense, they were within the system of the Ministry of Defence. That's true, but the composition of the civilian protection staff was appointed by the government as well -- the commanded, too, was appointed by the government. And this shows that it was a civilian body, although it might be strange given that there was a commander, given that it is called a staff, et cetera. But the assumption was that they operated in exceptional circumstances, or among other things, they would operate in exceptional circumstances, and then it was necessary to have a clear chain of command. I assume that is the reason for which the terms command and staff were used, but otherwise, according to its composition, its responsibilities, et cetera, this body was without a doubt a civilian body.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I would now like to move to another area you cover in your report and that is the proclamation of a state of war, and one issue which you cover, namely the adoption of a platform by the Presidency. Can you provide the Trial Chamber with some information in respect of the proclamation of a state of war and the adoption of the platform?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: By virtual proclaiming a state of war one could see that the circumstances were exceptional. The idea of state of the war means that it is necessary to mobilise all the men and all the other resources for the defence of the country. Naturally you can mobilise people. You can organise them to carry out a certain objective if you clearly define the objectives for which it is necessary to organise oneself. And I think that this is why the Presidency platform was of exceptional importance. In a certain sense, it provided a motive, the political basis. If you have a look at the contents of the platform, you'll see that this platform affirms the values upon which the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina is based. The principle of national equality is emphasised, the principle of democratic institutions and relations is emphasised, human rights and freedoms are guaranteed. And I want you to pay attention to one fact in particular. In that document which proclaims state of war, the Presidency clearly state that had they were in favour of a peaceful solution of the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and they even mentioned the principles that the Presidency would abide by in order to find a peaceful solution to the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. order to deal with the crisis in the former Yugoslavia. It's not strange that the Presidency required that if further discussions were to be held the legal authorities had to be respected. It was necessary to cease all hostilities. It was necessary to prosecute war criminals. And there are other factors that were mentioned that were necessary if there is to be a peace process. And naturally the Presidency was demonstrating that it was ready to participate in international attempts to solve the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, if I may consider myself as a -- someone who can analyse these events, they went further than the constitutional solutions from 1992. In order to lay to rest the objections that there was an international conflict in Bosnia, the Presidency mentioned certain solutions, announced certain solutions that the purpose of which was to confirm the idea of nationality equality. At the beginning of my testimony I mentioned the structure of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I said there were two Chambers, Chamber of Representatives and the Chamber of municipalities. This platform made the following proposal and naturally this wasn't contained in the constitution but they announced the council of peoples within the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And the members of the constituent peoples were supposed to be co-represented and vital national interests were to be protected within that system. So that was a response to the specific situation. And apart from this defence force in Bosnia and Herzegovina, it was necessary to support these constitutional categories that I mentioned earlier on. And the principle of national equality was to be emphasised more than in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I would now like to move to a different topic which is the judiciary in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and I refer you to paragraph 93 and following of your report. In your report, you explain that the civilian judiciary was as follows: Misdemeanour courts at the lowest level, followed by municipal court or basic court, normally seated in each municipality, but of course there were a lesser number of courts than there were of municipalities, followed by the higher court which could either be a first instance court or an appeals court for the municipal court, followed by the Supreme Court, which was the level of appeal for the higher court and some duties at the first instance but nothing to do with criminal law. Is this the way the judiciary functioned in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Yes. I briefly referred to the structure of the judiciary when I was describing the three branches of power. I mentioned the courts that existed. Naturally the judicial system included these lower or, rather, basic courts, which were the first-level ones, the first-level courts that dealt with criminal cases and civil cases of lesser importance. Then there was the higher court, which would deal with appeals against decisions rendered by the lower courts. But it also functioned as a first-level court in cases that were more serious. Appeals against their decisions would be referred to the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is the second-level court for criminal cases and civil cases. And the most serious crimes would be dealt with by this court when it came to appeals, and they would render final decisions on such cases. This Supreme Court had one additional function, and that was to control the executive bodies of power. So certain documents from the government or from ministries or other BH bodies could be controlled by the Supreme Court only in order to ensure that the constitution was respected in those documents. If the constitutionality or legal nature of a document, a decree, et cetera, was in question, then as is the case in all other countries throughout the world, the supreme -- the Constitutional Court deals with such issues. The Constitutional Court ensures that documents abide by the -- by general acts of general documents, whereas the Supreme Court deals with individual documents. In addition to this structure, we have the public prosecutor's office, and in criminal cases has the responsibility to carry out investigations, to request that investigations be carried out, to bring indictments and to do everything else prescribed by the law. One should not forget to mention misdemeanour courts, which one could call police courts. As a rule, they are part of the administrative authorities because they deal with minor offences against law and order, minor traffic violations, minor traffic offences. So crimes that don't present such a danger to society. So these courts don't really have the same status as regular courts as far as their responsibilities are concerned, because their jurisdiction is limited by misdemeanors. It's a different case in wartime. This is a new case, because -- this is a different situation, because military and district courts and district military prosecutor's office come into the system, are introduced into the system. Their purpose is primarily to protect values that have to be protected for the country, and they are part of the regular judicial authorities, because appeals against the decisions of the District Military Court are referred to the regular Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina and this ensures that the law is applied in the same way in civilian and in military courts. What is specific is that it has a specific nature when it comes to its real, its actual jurisdiction. But as far as the procedure is concerned and the guarantees for a fair trial, military courts are in no way different than civilian courts. It's true that judges at military courts are appointed by the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina but at a proposal from the minister of defence. And naturally junction ever district courts are appointed in this manner. It is necessary to distinguish the competence of military and regular courts but I've tried to provide you with a detailed explanation of this subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... one question I had for you was whether a member of the army could be tried before a civilian court, that is either the misdemeanour court, the municipal court or the higher court, and if so, in what situation?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Members of the military could be tried by civilian courts if they perpetrated a crime together with a civilian, and the regular court would have jurisdiction to deal with such a case. Naturally if a soldier committed an offence as a civilian, if he had been speeding or had disturbed the law and order, he would be tried by a regular court as a citizen. But in all other cases, military courts or, rather, the District Military Court was responsible for members of the military. But there is a second-level court, and I have emphasised this already.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, to provide you with an example, Professor, if a civilian and a member of the army are involved together in burning a house, which is a civilian house, and this has not -- no relation with the conflict, which type of court would handle this case?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: If we assume that it's not a military building of no interest for the defence of the country, then it would be the civilian court that would have responsibility to try the case, both for the civilian and for the member of the military.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Defence counsel please wait for the interpretation to finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and a member of the army are involved together in the killing of a civilian neighbour in a context that is not related to the armed conflict, which type of court would handle this situation?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: The answer would be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Professor. I will have to repeat my question which was not in the transcript, and my question at the beginning was if a civilian and a member of the army are involved together in the killing of a civilian neighbour in a context that is not related to the armed conflict, which type of court would handle this situation? And your answer was "it would be the same," and I take this to be a civilian court.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: That's correct. I didn't want to repeat the same thing again. If the case is of no military relevance, then the civilian court will try both the member of the military and the civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Professor, the issue of the special military court which you cover in your report, can you in a few words explain what was the special military court.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: In our language we'd say "special military court." It's quite clear that military units are often on the move. They're involved in military operations. Sometimes they don't have access to military courts or to military prosecutor's office. Yet the events of great importance for the conduct of military operations. For example, there's a rebellion in a military unit. Someone refuses to obey an order. Other soldiers are incited to rebel, et cetera, et cetera. These are very serious events and it's not possible to get involved in lengthy court proceedings. In such cases, according to a Presidency decree, the commanders of certain units were authorised to form these special military courts. Although that's not what it says in these regulations, but in theory I would say that these are ad hoc courts, temporary courts formed for a particular situation. In the documents I didn't notice that it was established as an independent institution. Such courts would be established for a specific situation, and the composition, the procedure was such that the reaction was prompt. It was rapid, expeditious, and it was necessary for such courts to be able to hand down the death penalty, naturally if they were justified in doing so. So theoretically speaking, I'd call it a court-martial. They could hand down the death penalty, and if they didn't hand down the death penalty, it was their responsibility to refer the case to the regular military prosecutor's office so that the prosecutor, the military prosecutor could continue to work on the case. However, it's necessary to point out that even if this court was a special court, this decree did provide certain minimal guarantees according to which the rights of the person concerned would not be violated, because there are two levels in the proceedings. There's a Chamber. It was necessary to have a defence council. That was obligatory. And a number of other documents also show that there's a minimum -- a minimum sort of democratic procedure was ensured. It's true to say that I couldn't come across any information showing whether this was a mass phenomenon. I don't know to what extent this was resorted to, but if it had been used extensively, I believe that there would have been media coverage of such events. But given the documents that I haven't seen, I didn't notice there was a mass appearance.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Hercegovina what possibilities existed in order to take measures and punish a member of the army for a violation?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: I would say that the situation was analogous to the situation in the civilian sector. Apart from the regular courts, there were misdemeanour courts. The army is a closed system, and the relations within the army are very clearly defined. The relations between soldiers, between soldiers and their officers, between the higher and lower command, their rules of conduct in the army, in their institutions in their units, et cetera, et cetera. So it's realistic to expect that these rules will sometimes be violated, and as a result there is a system for military misdemeanors, for disciplinary measures much, and as I have said at the beginning, this is not something that I dealt with in the first draft of my report, but I subsequently had a look at the rules that regulate this matter, and I noticed that in these cases the superior commander had certain authorities when it came to minor offences. In such cases, the commander could issue cautions, take certain measures, and the most severe penalty would be handed down, a 30-day prison sentence in a military prison. Then there was a disciplinary and misdemeanour court which could issue penalties for more serious misdemeanors. The penalties were more severe in such cases. For example, military promotion would be banned, sentences of up to 60 days in prison would be handed down, and there were certain other penalties that were more severe. And it's important to point out that in such misdemeanour proceedings, there would be a Bench dealing with the case, and the proceedings would take place at two levels. There was the possibility of appeal, in other words, and the Ministry of Defence formed a second-level disciplinary court which would hear appeals from these misdemeanour or disciplinary courts in military units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. On the basis of the answer you have just given concerning the types of courts which existed and where a member of the army could be the object of proceedings, I would like you to answer the following question: If someone wanted to know all proceedings instituted against the members of a military unit such as the 3rd Corps over a period of time, where would that person have to look?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: If I have understood your question correctly, it's necessary to bear in mind everything that I have been saying about the judicial system, both the military and civilian judicial system, because in one situation you might be held accountable before the civilian organs, and in another situation before military bodies, and disciplinary and criminal proceedings could be instituted. So in order to establish whether a member of the military was charged for some sort of offence, whether of a military or civilian nature, it's necessary to try and obtain the information on such an offence in a number of places. First one should see whether the person has been punished as a citizen for some misdemeanour. It's also necessary to see whether he appeared before regular courts with another civilian. It's necessary to establish whether the military prosecutor's office took any action against such an individual, and this should be found in the archives of these institutions. Then it would be necessary to go to the regular courts and to public Prosecutors to see whether this individual was charged together with some civilian. And then if we turn to the military bodies, it's necessary to see what sort of measures the commander took for disciplinary offences if any offences were reported. It's necessary to see what the military and misdemeanour court undertook with that respect, and it's necessary to see whether the military prosecutor took action against the individual in question. And then finally, it would be necessary to establish whether the District Military Court and finally the Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina had issued a legal decision with regard to the behaviour of such a member of the military. So you would require quite a lot of time in order to gather all that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I have one more question I wish to cover before we take the break, and that is with respect to the application of the Criminal Code in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I would like you to explain or provide details to what you say in your report as to which Criminal Code was in force in the period from 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: With a reservation that I am not a criminal law expert and that I haven't followed with the same amount of attention the developments in criminal law as was the case with constitutional matters, nevertheless I did look into the regulations linked to this question and I was able to establish the following: When Bosnia and Herzegovina became an independent and sovereign state with certain minor adjustments it took over the Criminal Code of the former SFRY but only the segment related to those criminal offences which have to do with violations of international obligations and those affecting state security or protection of the constitutional order. What the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia prescribed could by analogy be applied to Bosnia-Herzegovina which took over many international obligations. For instance, obligations under international humanitarian law and the Geneva Conventions in particular. And it was necessary for domestic laws to sanction violations of each of the provisions of the Geneva Conventions. And this was done very early on, at the very beginning of the armed conflict. And as I mention in the report, a decree law was passed and the takeover of the Criminal Code of Yugoslavia, and this was published in the Official Gazette number 2 in 1992, which means at the very beginning of the conflict. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. However, conscious of the fact that the danger for society of violations of the law are much graver in wartime, the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina have repeatedly strengthened sanctions that were prescribed for peacetime either in the Yugoslav Criminal Code or in the Criminal Code of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the substantive law which was adopted in the meantime. And by a decree passed at the beginning of the war, published in the Official Gazette number 11 through 1992, the penalties were increased for these mentioned criminal offences, and an additional penalty was introduced, that is the confiscation of property of those who in addition to regular penalties need to have their property confiscated. And it was also important, if a certain offence was committed with the same of spreading ethnic hatred and intolerance which was particularly important during the conflict, then the special qualification which was considered an aggravating factor was added, that is if such an offence was committed for -- out of ethnic hatred or to fan intolerance. So there were several instances of the authorities of Bosnia-Herzegovina taking over laws from the former Yugoslavia. For instance, the Official Gazette number 21 of 1992 also refers to stricter -- the introduction of stricter penalties. As for criminal procedural law, it was more or less taken over in its entirety from the former Yugoslavia, because procedure is procedure. It doesn't matter which country we're talking about, on condition that it was a democratic country providing guarantees that a normal democratic society provides. And that is why the Law on Criminal Procedure was taken over. And then later on it was adjusted to wartime conditions, because certain guarantees that are envisaged by criminal procedure are simply impossible to implement during wartime. Thus, for instance, the law and criminal procedure --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Professor, I think we will have to stop because we are running into the technical time that we have to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will need a maximum of ten to 15 minutes to finish with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] I will ask you during the break simply to look at the handout given to you. It's in the side of your documents. It's a handout like this. I would ask you during the break to look at documents 8, 9, 10, and 11, and the question will be whether this confirms what you were just explaining about the sanctions that could be awarded by the courts in wartime. Thank you very much, Professor?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have the break now, and we will resume at 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Welcome back, Professor. Just before we left, I asked you to take a look at documents 8, 9, 10, and 11. And my first question relates to the first three documents, 8, 9 and 10. I would like you to explain whether these three documents is what you were referring to when you said that the Presidency because in times of war wanted to give harsher penalties and sentences for a variety of crimes. Can you going over quickly documents 8, 9, and 10 and confirm that this is what you were referring to.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: If I'm looking at the right documents, in my view there's no doubt, in my opinion, that 9 and 10 is what I was referring to, probably 11 as well. But number 8 is a report only the Executive Board meeting of Bugojno municipality. That's number 8. Is that the document you're referring to? No. That's number 7. No. That's my mistake. Yes, from 8 onwards does relate to what we were talking about, regulations passed by the Presidency designed not only to issue harsher sentences but to introduce additional measures to sanction behaviour from which there was grave social danger. And in this first document there are eight new measures envisaged in addition to the penalty, dismissal from duties, stripping of rank, a ban of appearing in public. All this aimed to have a preventative effect and punish criminal behaviour more strictly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I would like you to look at document number 9, and inside this document to Article 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document I'm referring to, Mr. President, is a new document, and I ask the permission of the Chamber to use this document. It has been disclosed to the Prosecution. It is a document addressing the same issues as the two documents shown during the previous hearing, that is DH2042 ID and DH2043 ID, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution. No objection?

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English] Professor, if you can look at Article 2 of this decree law, and I will just read it in English where it says: "After Article 6, a new Article 6(A) and 6(B) are added, stating," and then we look at Article 6(A), "also a person who takes life of another because the national intolerance will be published for the criminal act of murder." Is this what you were referring to a little earlier when talking about intolerance and harsher penalties?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: I said that because we are dealing with an inter-ethnic conflict and to have a preventive effect, this criminal act, criminal offence was introduced, that is if a criminal offence is conducted prompted by the desire to spread ethnic hatred, and this provision confirms what I was saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And can you confirm, Professor, that the punishment of death was attributed to such a crime?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Yes. That would be the worst sentence that can be pronounced, which means that this offence was considered to be of the greatest social danger, the greatest threat to society.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Moving on to document number 11. Can you explain what this document is and the relation between these documents and the decree laws adopted by the Presidency before the 1st of June, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this document, unfortunately, is a new document which is not available in English or in French, and in view of its length, we were unable to have it translated for today's sitting. It is a document which the Chamber asked to see following the testimony of the previous witness, Judge Ahmetovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can ask the witness to tell us the title and date and identify the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [In English]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, can you identify this document and explain what the document does in relation to decree laws adopted by the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Before I answer this question, I should like to ask the interpreter or the registrar to increase the volume a little bit because I'm having difficulty hearing the translation. As for your question, in the theory of law and in comparative constitutional law, in all situations when the system envisages the introduction of special powers for the executive branch of government, it is democratic practice for those special powers to be used only exceptionally because -- when parliament cannot meet. As under conditions of a state of war, it was virtually impossible to convene such a large Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina, then the Presidency issued a number of decrees with the force of law. When the Assembly did meet in full, and this happened, according to this document, in June 1994, that was a superintendent for the Presidency to submit for ratification all decree laws which it had passed in the meantime. And we have here a list of all those decrees and other acts of the Presidency ending with number 364, which means that the Assembly ratified all laws listed here whereby they became laws in the strict sense of the word. If there were Presidency acts which are not listed here, those acts cease to be valid as of this moment. Of course, I didn't compare this list with all the acts passed by the Presidency, but I assumed that virtually all the Presidency decisions taken were ratified by the Assembly in June 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I now move on to asking your opinion on the basis of the system of authorities or of government that you explained in your report and ask you your opinion on a few issues, the first question being whether in your opinion the system in place in 1992 and 1993 ensured the civilian control over the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I didn't hear the first part of your question. I'm afraid I didn't hear the first part of the question because the volume wasn't switched on. I'm still having some difficulties because there's a buzzing sound, but I understood the question, whether within the system that I have described, whether civilian control over the armed forces functioned. Was that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Judging by the documents I had available to me, I was able to come to the conclusion that during this period of time there was civilian control over the armed forces and that it was implemented according to the order which I presented a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. My second question relates to the civilian bodies during the period 1992 and 1993. In your report, you have highlighted a number of problems which affected the work of these organisations. I with like to know if in your opinion the civilian organisation and bodies continued to function despite these problems.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: The theory of comparative constitutional law views criteria of legitimacy and legality of institutions in wartime are reduced to some extent as required by the circumstances. In my previous presentation and in my report in much greater detail, I cautioned and drew attention to the problems encountered by the civilian authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I think that basically the legality of institutions was preserved throughout this period and which, perhaps, could be confirmed by the peace agreement for Bosnia and Herzegovina which confirms the international legal continuity and the internal legal continuity of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question is whether on the basis of the system in place in 1992 and 1993 the 3rd Corps of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina could exercise control or influence the work of the judiciary, namely the District Military Court.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Referring exclusively to constitutional law and the system, there were no systemic possibilities for any military influence over civilian courts. I am not claiming that there may not have been certain instances in practice. It's not up to me to speak about facts, but I am speaking about the system as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question is whether the system in place in 1992 and 1993, in your opinion prevented the 3rd Corps from exercising command and control over the civilian police other than in exceptional circumstances as approved by the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Again, from the standpoint of the system, there are no regular channels on influence of the military structure over the civilian police. The exception is the Presidency decision, which needs to be looked into in each particular case, that is whether there was any such decision by the Presidency and whether it was implemented. So again we come to a difference between the system and the actual facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My next question, Professor, is whether the system in place in 1992 and 1993 prevented the 3rd Corps of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to exercise any command and control or influence over civilian institutions including, for example, the municipal War Presidency or the civilian protection staff.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, may I interrupt. We're not getting the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises. The volume was not switched on. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can you deal with the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm having a problem with the sound.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not switch on her microphone. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's try again. Mr. Bourgon, will you put that question again and see whether it works.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Professor, the question was as follows: Whether the system in place in 1993 and towards, of course, the end of 1992, prevented the 3rd Corps of the army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to exercise any command and control or influence over civilian institutions including, for example, the municipal War Presidency or the civilian protection staff.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: I seem to understand that there were two questions, whether there was any obstacle in achieving the system of command within the military structure starting from civilian control by the Presidency down to military units. Of course there is not something I did not investigate in actual fact but only how things were regulated by laws. And as I said at the beginning of today's hearing, this was regulated in some detail. As for the second part of the question, whether the military had influence over the civilian authorities, be they municipal or district authorities or civilian protection staff, in the system there is no possibility of influence. But in actual fact, since the Staff Commander was a member of the municipal Presidency under the old system and not in the new, I don't see how it could bring any influence to bear over the civilian structure of authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: In your report, Professor, you highlight orders issued by the commander of the 3rd Corps, which highlight the fact that there was a clear distinction to be made between the civilian police and the military police. My question is whether on the documents you have seen you can say that there was a practice amongst all units of the 3rd Corps to issue such orders and whether the orders issued corresponded to the applicable law at the time.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: You're asking me a very complicated question in view of my position. I didn't have insight in a lot of documents of the 3rd Corps, but I did encounter documents in which the 3rd Corps Commander made a clear distinction in a letter addressed to the security services centre in Zenica. He said in that document quite clearly that the army had completed its military operations and withdrawn from the area, and now that it was the duty of the security services centre to take over responsibility for any disorders. So it follows from this that he understood quite clearly what everyone should do under such circumstances. Or we mentioned the example when they need to act together, that is the military and civilian police when there is coordinated action between the military and civilian official who is responsible for these matters and a -- clear instructions were given as to how the civilian and the military police should act. Now, whether the other commanders within the 3rd Corps acted in that manner, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. You mentioned the word "coordinated action between the military and civilian officials who were responsible for these matters." In your report, you talk about the principle of cooperation, which is something that has evolved over time and which led to the issuance of an instruction at the end of 1993. Can you explain this principle and how it worked?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: As in the introduction, we spoke about the functioning of the military vertical chain of command and the functioning of the civilian authorities on the other hand, including the Ministry of Internal Affairs. It can clearly be seen from this that the responsibilities are clearly Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. designated with respect to the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, at lower levels those authorities may engage in cooperation, and I mentioned with respect to the security services centre or the defence staff it was their duty to provide information about the situation in their area of responsibility, but they could not receive orders from local or regional civilian authorities, orders to military or police structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. My next question deals with the relationship between civilian authorities and the army but in the other way, and more specifically whether the system in place created the possibility for civilian institutions such as the War Presidency of a municipality to exercise some type of influence or command and control over units of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: In view of everything presented so far in explanation of the system that was functioning, such a possibility did not exist, though of course if we recall that in the common state of Yugoslavia, at the level of municipal presidencies and Territorial Defence staffs, there was a connection between the civilian and military authorities, and that in people's consciousness there may have been a feeling that the civilian authorities should have some influence, but systemically there was not envisaged. In reviewing the documentation that I had at my disposal, I came across certain instances when the civilian authorities endeavoured to impose not only on military authorities but also on judiciary bodies which should be fully independent their influence. And a moment ago when we were looking at the documents on footnotes or, rather, the attachments, in document number 8 we have an example when the Executive Board of Bugojno suggested to misdemeanour courts how to impose stricter sentences or when they said that certain contracts approved by the court should be

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: I came across another document from Bugojno in which the local SDA party organisation - I may not remember the exact term used - whether it was -- it gave its approval or it was merely consulted as to who would be appointed to the position of commander of the local military units. So these are examples which show that there may have been deviations in practice, but according to the system that I have described, such practice was illegal.

utterances.speaker: THE EXECUTIVE BODIES SUCH
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. I just have one last question for you. It is a topic which you cover in your report towards the end when you discuss the Vance-Owen Plan as well as the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan. And I would simply like without going over everything you have mentioned in your report about these two plans, provide the Trial Chamber with an idea of the context in which these plans were negotiated, their impacts on the functioning of the system in place, and what happened in both cases.

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Plan was negotiated for a long time, and it was signed on the 2nd of May, 1993. But representatives of the Serbian Democratic Party expressed certain reservations. They said that their signature would be valid if the Assembly of the so-called Republika Srpska confirmed such a signature. Such confirmation was not provided subsequently, and in a certain sense the Vance-Owen Plan fell through. This plan envisaged the establishment of ten provinces in Bosnia and Herzegovina. It envisaged amending the constitutional structure of Bosnia-Herzegovina and envisaged ten provinces. And the intransitory solutions were interesting. The solutions it concerned the deployment of military forces when the Vance-Owen Plan was being implemented. It stated which provinces would be under the exclusive control of the Republika Srpska army, which ones under the exclusive control of the HVO, and which ones under the exclusive control of the BH army. According to the chart we have attached, provinces 8, 9 and 10 were provinces in which the HVO and the BH army were to play a joint role. And in the field, this was taken to mean that certain forces should establish military authority as soon as possible, military control over as much territory as possible. And according to a record or an order, a decision from the War Presidency in Travnik, in that document we can see that two days after the Vance-Owen Plan had been signed an attempt was made to restructure the municipal authorities and to establish a municipal Presidency in which Croats and Muslims would participate on an equal footing. In a certain sense, this meant that this would ensure the direct implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan. According to the Owen and Stoltenberg plan, this plan was a result of the peace initiative of the then-President Tudjman and Milosevic. They suggested that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, three national republics should be formed. On the basis of the principle that wherever one of the peoples was in the majority, that is where that people should have its republic. It would be called the Croatian republic, the Bosniak republic, and the Serbian republic. And Bosnia and Herzegovina would in fact have disappeared as a result. It would just -- it would have just been turned into or transformed into an unstable union of three republics that had the responsibility of international recognition and also the possibility of seceding from such a union. Naturally, this plan was never implemented, because all the parties had certain reservations in relation to the plan. But it was the most fatal plan for the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina and for a peace solution. But it also had certain results in the field in that there were attempts to legalise the military situation in the field and to ensure that one had control over as much territory as possible. We know that the Owen-Stoltenberg Plan was never in fact implemented. It was discussed after the Vance-Owen Plan fell through. That from autumn 1993 up till the end of 1993, because at the beginning of 1994, intensive preparations were under way for the Washington Agreement, and that is when the USA became seriously engaged in the peace process. And through the Washington Agreement, the basis for a peace plan, for a solution to the crisis in Bosnia-Herzegovina was laid.

utterances.speaker: THE EXECUTIVE BODIES SUCH
utterances.text: I may have, Professor, one more question for you in relation to your last answer. Were you involved in the discussions and the negotiations leading to the Vance-Owen Plan, and if so, are you in a position to provide an opinion on the attitude of the HVO towards the implementation of this plan?

utterances.speaker: KASIM TRNKA
utterances.text: Well, in fact I would be changing my position as a witness when answering this question. I think I should continue to testify as an expert witness, to testify about the contents of that plan. I was, as I have said at the beginning of my testimony, that quite by chance I was there as an expert. That was my function in the course of those negotiations, and naturally I had nothing to do with the political decisions. But there is no doubt that the HVO with regard to areas where there was a common interest, they were interested in taking over power in certain areas. In certain municipalities, as far as I know, this was in fact done.

utterances.speaker: THE EXECUTIVE BODIES SUCH
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Professor. I have no more questions at this stage. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, that concludes the examination-in-chief of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. I'll now give the floor to Mr. Kubura's Defence team if they have any questions for this witness, for the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This was -- or he is an expert witness for both Defence teams, and we have no questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You have no other questions, no additional questions to put to the expert witness. It's 20 to seven. We have another 20 minutes. Would the Prosecution prefer to commence their cross-examination now or would you prefer to wait until tomorrow morning? Ms. Benjamin, it's your choice.

utterances.speaker: MS. HENRY-BENJAMIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would prefer the opportunity to start afresh tomorrow morning, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Trnka, Professor, Defence counsel has just completed its examination-in-chief. The second stage is the so-called cross-examination, which will commence tomorrow morning, and it is Ms. Benjamin who will be conducting the cross-examination. As you have taken the solemn declaration, you did so at the beginning of this afternoon, you are now a witness testifying in the interest of justice. You are no longer a witness for the Defence, because you are a witness who is testifying in order to establish the truth. This means that you should not meet anyone until the hearing commences tomorrow. You shouldn't meet any representatives of the Defence or of the Prosecution. I just wanted to point this minor procedural matter out to you. In a few minutes we will adjourn. Please contact the Victims and Witnesses Unit to ensure that you are here at the beginning of the morning since the hearing will commence at 9.00. And I believe that we should be able to conclude your testimony here at The Hague by 1.45 tomorrow unless there are other questions or Judges' questions that will mean that we have to work beyond this time. I will see everyone tomorrow at the hearing at 9.00.
